text: Principio quoniam tenuem constare minutis corporibus docui multoque minoribus esse principiis factam quam liquidus umor aquai aut nebula aut fumus — nam longe mobilitate praestat et a tenui causa magis icta movetur — nunc igitur quoniam quassatis undique vasis diffluere umorem et laticem discedere cernis, et nebula ac fumus quoniam discedit in auras, crede animam quoque diffundi multoque perire ocius et citius dissolvi in corpora prima, cum semel ex hominis membris ablata recessit.
difficulty: Lucretius's argument for the soul's mortality via analogy to fluids and vapors. The extended period spans 15 lines with a single main clause (crede) delayed by multiple subordinate causal clauses (quoniam...quoniam). 'liquidus umor aquai' uses the archaic genitive '-ai' for '-ae.' 'quassatis undique vasis' (when vessels are shattered on all sides) is the ablative absolute grounding the analogy. The soul-as-vapor metaphor requires tracking three parallel dissolutions (water, mist, soul).
translation_A: At the beginning, I taught that the thin consists of small bodies and that it is made of much smaller principles than the liquid moisture of water, mist, or smoke—for it far excels in mobility and is moved more by a slight cause. Now, therefore, since you see the moisture flowing out and the liquid departing from shattered vessels everywhere, and the mist and smoke departing into the air, believe that the soul also spreads out and perishes much more quickly and is more swiftly dissolved into the first bodies, once it has been taken away and departed from the human limbs.
translation_D: At the outset, since I have taught that the fine and subtle nature of matter consists of small bodies, and that the first principles (atoms) are far smaller than liquid moisture, water vapor, or smoke—for they excel much more in mobility and are more readily set in motion by a subtle cause—now, therefore, since you observe that moisture and fluid are flowing out from shattered vessels on all sides, and since the cloud and smoke are dispersing into the air, believe that the soul, too, is dispersed and perishes much more quickly, dissolving into the first bodies (atoms) once it has been removed from the human limbs.

annotations.meaning: thin, subtle, or fine (referring to the nature of matter)
annotations.significance: This term is central to Epicurean physics, emphasizing the idea that matter is composed of very small, subtle particles. It underscores the concept of material fineness and its implications for understanding physical phenomena.

annotations.meaning: first principles or fundamental elements (here, atoms)
annotations.significance: In Epicurean philosophy, 'principia' refers to the indivisible atoms that constitute all matter. This term is crucial for understanding the foundational theory of Epicurean physics, which posits that everything is composed of these fundamental, eternal elements.

This phrase illustrates the process of dispersion or dissolution, a key concept in Epicurean explanations of physical phenomena. It highlights the transient nature of composite substances, which are subject to disintegration.

This term represents a specific type of fluid or binding substance in the text. Its use here helps to contrast the stability of composite bodies with the inherent instability of their constituent parts, reinforcing the Epicurean argument about the impermanence of non-atomic substances.

annotations.meaning: believe that the soul also disperses
annotations.significance: This phrase is pivotal for understanding the Epicurean view of the soul. It suggests that the soul, like other physical substances, is composed of atoms and is therefore subject to dispersion and dissolution, contradicting the idea of an immortal soul.

This phrase encapsulates the Epicurean belief in the ultimate dissolution of all composite things into their atomic constituents. It emphasizes the materialistic and reductionist worldview central to Epicurean philosophy.

text: Illud in his quoque te rebus cognoscere avemus, corpora cum deorsum rectum per inane feruntur ponderibus propriis, incerto tempore ferme incertisque locis spatio depellere paulum, tantum quod momen mutatum dicere possis. Quod nisi declinare solerent, omnia deorsum imbris uti guttae caderent per inane profundum nec foret offensus natus nec plaga creata principiis; ita nihil umquam natura creasset.
difficulty: Lucretius's clinamen (atomic swerve) doctrine — the most controversial passage in Epicurean physics. 'incerto tempore ferme incertisque locis' (at roughly uncertain times and uncertain places) introduces indeterminacy. 'tantum quod momen mutatum dicere possis' (only so much that you could call it a changed motion) minimizes the swerve. 'imbris uti guttae' (like drops of rain) provides the counterfactual image. 'offensus...nec plaga' (collision nor blow) explains why the swerve is cosmogonically necessary.
translation_A: We have in these things also to recognize that when bodies are borne straight downward through the void by their own weights, they are for the most part deflected from their course in uncertain times and uncertain places by a small amount, just enough to allow you to speak of a changed direction. For if they were not accustomed to swerve, all things would fall downward like drops of rain through the profound void, and neither collision nor blow would have been created among the first beginnings; thus, nature would have created nothing.
translation_D: In these matters, too, we observe this (truth), that when bodies are borne straight downward through the void by their own weights (ponderibus propriis), they are for the most part deflected from their course (spatio depellere paulum) at an uncertain time (incerto tempore) and uncertain places (incertisque locis), just enough that you could speak of a changed motion (momen mutatum). For if they were not accustomed to swerve (declinare), all things would fall downward through the profound void like raindrops (imbris uti guttae), nor would the collision (plaga) of first principles (principiis) have been created, nor the nature of compound bodies (offensus natus) have arisen; thus, nature would have created nothing (nihil umquam natura creasset).

annotations.significance: This phrase highlights the natural tendency of atoms to move downward due to their inherent weight, a central concept in Epicurean physics.
This phrase emphasizes the unpredictability of atomic motion, which is crucial for understanding the Epicurean concept of the atomic swerve (clinamen).
This term refers to the fundamental atoms, the basic building blocks of the universe in Epicurean philosophy, and their role in the formation of the world.
This phrase describes the slight deviation in atomic motion (the swerve), which is essential for collisions and the creation of the world, countering strict determinism.
This term refers to the collisions between atoms resulting from the swerve, which are necessary for the formation of complex structures and the world as we know it.

text: Sic in amore Venus simulacris ludit amantis, nec satiare queunt spectando corpora coram nec manibus quicquam teneris abradere membris possunt errantes incerti corpore toto. Denique cum membris conlatis flore fruuntur aetatis, iam cum praesagit gaudia corpus atque in eost Venus ut muliebria conserat arva, adfigunt avide corpus iunguntque salivas oris et inspirant pressantes dentibus ora, nequiquam, quoniam nihil inde abradere possunt nec penetrare et abire in corpus corpore toto.
difficulty: Lucretius's devastating materialist analysis of erotic desire. 'simulacris ludit amantis' (Venus toys with lovers through images) reduces love to atomic simulacra. 'nec satiare queunt...nec...abradere' (neither satisfy nor scrape away anything) exposes desire's futility. 'muliebria conserat arva' (sow feminine fields) is a striking agricultural metaphor for sex. 'nequiquam' (in vain) is the philosophical punchline. The passage requires understanding Epicurean perception theory to grasp why physical contact cannot satisfy.
translation_A: Thus in love, Venus plays with the likenesses of lovers, nor can they sate themselves by gazing at bodies before them, nor can they snatch anything from the tender limbs with wandering, uncertain hands over the entire body. Finally, when they enjoy the bloom of youth with limbs brought together, now when the body forebodes joys and Venus, as in a feminine field, sows the seeds, they eagerly fasten their bodies and join the saliva of the mouth, and they breathe into the mouths pressed by teeth, in vain, since they can snatch nothing from there, nor penetrate and depart into the body with the entire body.
translation_D: Thus Venus plays with lovers through statues or images (simulacris), nor can they satisfy their desire by gazing at the bodies before them, nor can they scrape anything off (abradere) with their tender hands from the limbs, wandering uncertainly over the whole body. Finally, when they enjoy the flower of youth with their limbs brought together, and when the body already anticipates the joys, and Venus, like a farmer sowing feminine fields (muliebria), plants the seeds, they eagerly fasten their bodies together, joining their mouths and breathing into each other, pressing with their teeth, yet to no purpose (nequiquam), since they can neither scrape anything off nor penetrate and pass through into the body with their whole body.

annotations.significance: Represents the elusive and unattainable nature of desire, as Venus toys with lovers using mere images or representations of what they long for.

annotations.meaning: to scrape off or rub away
annotations.significance: Highlights the futility of physical attempts to satisfy desire, as lovers cannot truly 'scrape away' or consume the object of their longing.
Emphasizes the all-consuming nature of physical desire, as the entire body is involved in the pursuit of pleasure, yet satisfaction remains elusive.
Used metaphorically to describe Venus sowing the 'fields' of passion, symbolizing the natural yet unattainable aspect of desire.
Illustrates the intense physical and emotional connection sought by lovers, as they try to merge their very beings, though ultimately in vain.
Summarizes the central theme of the passage: the futility of attempting to satisfy desire, as true union and fulfillment are impossible.

text: Nec tamen undique corporea stipata tenentur omnia natura; namque est in rebus inane. Nunc age, res quoniam docui non posse creari de nihilo neque item genitas ad nil revocari, ne qua forte tamen coeptes diffidere dictis, quod nequeunt oculis rerum primordia cerni, accipe praeterea quae corpora tute necessest confiteare esse in rebus nec posse videri.
difficulty: Lucretius's argument for void and invisible atoms. 'undique corporea stipata...natura' (packed on all sides by corporeal nature) describes a hypothetical plenum. 'namque est in rebus inane' (for there is void in things) is one of the most consequential philosophical statements in Latin. 'genitas ad nil revocari' (things created cannot be called back to nothing) compresses the conservation principle. 'confiteare' is the subjunctive of 'confiteor' in an unusually philosophical usage.
translation_A: And yet, not all things are held in a corporeal embrace everywhere in nature; for there is void in things. Come now, since I have taught that things cannot be created from nothing and likewise cannot be reduced to nothing, lest you by chance begin to distrust my words because the first beginnings of things cannot be seen with the eyes, accept moreover those bodies which you must confess exist in things and cannot be seen.
translation_D: Yet not all of nature is everywhere filled with corporeal substance; for there exists in things the void. Come now, since I have shown that things cannot be created from nothing and likewise cannot be reduced to nothing, lest you by chance begin to distrust my words because the first beginnings of things cannot be seen with the eyes, take also this point: there are bodies that you must necessarily acknowledge to exist in things, and yet they cannot be seen.

annotations.significance: Central to Epicurean physics, 'inane' refers to the void or empty space that exists alongside matter. It is a key concept in the argument against the idea that the universe is entirely filled with physical substance.
A rhetorical address to the reader, encouraging engagement with the argument. It reflects the didactic tone of the poem, guiding the audience through the philosophical explanation.
Refers to the philosophical concept of creation from nothing, which Epicurus argues is impossible. This is a cornerstone of his materialist worldview.

annotations.meaning: things that have been born or produced
annotations.significance: Highlights the Epicurean belief in the indestructibility of matter. Things cannot be reduced to nothing because matter is eternal and only changes form.
A central concept in Epicurean atomism, referring to the indivisible particles that make up all things. They are the fundamental building blocks of the universe.

Emphasizes the invisibility of the atomic particles to the naked eye, a key challenge in Epicurean epistemology. It underscores the limitations of human perception in understanding the physical world.

text: Non enim hanc solam sequimur, quae suavitate aliqua naturam ipsam movet et cum iucunditate quadam percipitur sensibus, sed maximam voluptatem illam habemus, quae percipitur omni dolore detracto. Itaque non placuit Epicuro medium esse quiddam inter dolorem et voluptatem; illud enim ipsum, quod quibusdam medium videretur, cum omni dolore careret, non modo voluptatem esse, verum etiam summam voluptatem.
difficulty: Cicero's presentation of Epicurean katastematic pleasure. 'quae suavitate aliqua naturam ipsam movet' (which moves nature itself by some sweetness) defines kinetic pleasure. 'omni dolore detracto' (with all pain removed) defines the higher catastematic pleasure. 'non placuit Epicuro medium esse quiddam' (Epicurus did not accept there to be something intermediate) rejects a third state between pleasure and pain. The nested relative clauses and indirect speech require careful syntactic parsing.
translation_A: For we do not pursue this alone, which by some charm stirs nature itself and is perceived with a certain pleasantness by the senses, but we hold that the greatest pleasure is the one perceived when all pain is removed. Therefore, it did not please Epicurus that there is some middle state between pain and pleasure; for that very thing, which seemed to some to be a middle state, when it is free from all pain, is not only pleasure but also the greatest pleasure.
translation_D: For we do not pursue only this pleasure, which moves nature itself with some degree of sweetness and is perceived with a certain delight by the senses, but we consider that pleasure to be the greatest which is perceived when all pain is removed. Therefore, it did not please Epicurus that there should be a middle state between pain and pleasure; for that which seemed to some to be a middle state, being free from all pain, is not only pleasure but even the greatest pleasure.

annotations.meaning: For we do not pursue only this pleasure, which moves nature itself with some degree of sweetness and is perceived with a certain delight by the senses.
annotations.significance: This phrase introduces the Epicurean distinction between two types of pleasure: the active, sensual pleasure and the passive absence of pain. It sets up the argument that Epicureanism values the latter more highly.

annotations.meaning: pleasure (specifically the absence of physical pain and mental distress)
annotations.significance: In Epicurean philosophy, 'voluptas' often refers to the absence of pain rather than hedonistic indulgence. This term is central to understanding the ethical argument of the passage.

This phrase emphasizes the Epicurean ideal of freedom from physical and mental suffering as the highest form of pleasure. It underscores the idea that true happiness comes from the absence of pain, not from active indulgence.

annotations.meaning: a middle state between pain and pleasure
annotations.significance: Epicurus rejected the idea of a neutral state between pain and pleasure. This term highlights his argument that the absence of pain is itself a form of pleasure, not a separate state.

This term emphasizes the Epicurean view that the absence of pain is not just a form of pleasure but the highest and most desirable form of it. It underscores the central tenet of Epicurean ethics in this passage.

text: Constitit autem fere inter omnes id, in quo prudentia versaretur et quod assequi vellet, aptum et accommodatum naturae esse oportere et tale, ut ipsum per se invitaret et alliceret appetitum animi, quem ὁρμήν Graeci vocant. Quid autem sit, quod ita moveat itaque a natura in primo ortu appetatur, non constat deque eo est inter philosophos, cum summum bonum exquiritur, omnis dissensio.
difficulty: Cicero's mapping of Greek ὁρμή onto Latin appetitus animi. The first sentence contains four nested subordinate clauses before the main verb 'constitit.' 'aptum et accommodatum naturae' (fitted and adapted to nature) encodes the Stoic oikeiosis doctrine. 'in primo ortu appetatur' (is sought in the first origin) refers to the cradle argument. 'cum summum bonum exquiritur' inserts an ablative absolute into already complex indirect speech. This is among the densest philosophical prose in Latin.
translation_A: It is agreed, however, almost among all that what prudence would concern itself with and seek to attain ought to be suitable and in harmony with nature, and of such a kind that it would invite and entice the mind's desire, which the Greeks call ὁρμή. But what this thing is, which moves us in such a way and is desired by nature from the very beginning, is not agreed upon, and there is complete disagreement among philosophers when the highest good is being sought.
translation_D: It has been established, moreover, almost universally among all that the object on which practical wisdom would deliberate and which it would wish to attain ought to be suited and adapted to nature, and of such a kind that it would invite and entice the soul's desire by itself, which the Greeks call ὁρμήν (hormēn). But as to what this is, which so moves and is thus desired by nature from the very first beginning, there is no agreement, and concerning this, when the highest good (summum bonum) is being sought, there is complete disagreement among philosophers.

annotations.meaning: Practical wisdom or prudent judgment, guiding human action and decision-making.

text: Quod semper movetur, aeternum est; quod autem motum adfert alicui quodque ipsum agitatur aliunde, quando finem habet motus, vivendi finem habeat necesse est. Solum igitur, quod se ipsum movet, quia numquam deseritur a se, numquam ne moveri quidem desinit. Principii autem nulla est origo; nam e principio oriuntur omnia, ipsum autem nulla ex re alia nasci potest.
difficulty: Cicero's Latin rendering of Plato's Phaedrus argument for soul immortality via self-motion. 'Quod semper movetur aeternum est' translates Plato's ἀεικίνητον. 'quodque ipsum agitatur aliunde' (that which is itself set in motion from elsewhere) uses the passive with ablative of agent. 'numquam ne moveri quidem desinit' (never even ceases to be moved) stacks intensifiers. The passage is essentially a philosophical translation exercise, reproducing Greek metaphysics in Latin syntax.
translation_A: What is always in motion is eternal; but that which imparts motion to something else and is itself moved by another thing, when it has an end of motion, must have an end of living. Therefore, only that which moves itself, because it is never deserted by itself, never ceases to move. However, the principle has no origin; for all things arise from the principle, but it itself cannot be born from any other thing.
translation_D: What is always in motion is eternal; for that which imparts motion to something else, and is itself moved by something else, when its motion comes to an end, must necessarily come to the end of its existence. Only that which moves itself, because it is never deserted by itself, never even ceases from motion. The first principle, however, has no origin; for all things arise from the first principle, but it itself cannot be born from any other thing.

annotations.significance: This phrase introduces the central argument about the nature of motion and eternity, linking perpetual motion to the eternal nature of the soul.
This term is crucial as it directly ties the concept of perpetual motion to eternity, a key tenet in Platonic philosophy regarding the immortality of the soul.

text: Optime autem societas hominum coniunctioque servabitur, si, ut quisque erit coniunctissimus, ita in eum benignitatis plurimum conferetur. Sed quae naturae principia sint communitatis et societatis humanae, repetendum videtur altius. Est enim primum quod cernitur in universi generis humani societate; eius autem vinculum est ratio et oratio, quae docendo, discendo, communicando, disceptando, iudicando conciliat inter se homines coniungitque naturali quadam societate.
difficulty: Cicero's Stoic-influenced theory of natural human community. 'ut quisque erit coniunctissimus ita...plurimum' (as each person is most closely connected, so the most...) encodes a proportionality principle. 'ratio et oratio' (reason and speech) is a characteristically Ciceronian pair linking intellect to language. The five gerunds 'docendo, discendo, communicando, disceptando, iudicando' enumerate the activities constituting civil society. 'naturali quadam societate' adds philosophical weight through 'quadam' (a certain kind of).
translation_A: The society and union of humans will be best preserved if, as each person is most closely connected, so the greatest kindness is bestowed upon them. But it seems necessary to revisit more deeply the natural principles of community and human society. For the first thing observed in the society of the entire human race is that its bond is reason and speech, which, through teaching, learning, communicating, discussing, and judging, bring people together and unite them in a natural kind of society.
translation_D: But the fellowship and union of human beings will be best preserved if, to the extent that someone is most closely connected, so much benevolence is bestowed upon them. Yet, it seems necessary to revisit more deeply the natural principles of community and human society. For what is first perceived is in the society of the entire human race; its bond, moreover, is reason and speech, which, through teaching, learning, sharing, discussing, and judging, reconcile and join human beings among themselves in a natural kind of fellowship.

This concept underscores the ethical foundation of Stoic thought, emphasizing that benevolence is essential for fostering strong social connections and maintaining harmony within a community.

text: Nam nisi multorum praeceptis multisque litteris mihi ab adulescentia suasissem, nihil esse in vita magno opere expetendum nisi laudem atque honestatem, in ea autem persequenda omnis cruciatus corporis, omnia pericula mortis atque exsili parvi esse ducenda, numquam me pro salute vestra in tot ac tantas dimicationes atque in hos profligatorum hominum cotidianos impetus obiecissem.
difficulty: One of the longest and most complex periods in Cicero's forensic oratory. The protasis (nisi...suasissem) contains two indirect statements (nihil esse...omnis cruciatus...parvi esse ducenda). The apodosis (numquam me...obiecissem) delays the main verb to the final word. 'profligatorum hominum' (ruined/abandoned men) carries strong moral censure. The sentence argues that literature motivated Cicero's public service — a politically audacious claim in a courtroom.
translation_A: For unless I had persuaded myself from youth, based on the teachings of many and much literature, that nothing in life is greatly to be desired except praise and honor, and that in pursuing these, all bodily suffering, all dangers of death and exile, are to be considered of little account, I would never have thrown myself into so many and such great struggles, and into the daily attacks of these wicked men, for the sake of your safety.
translation_D: For unless, from my youth, I had persuaded myself, through the precepts of many and the writings of many, that nothing in life is to be eagerly sought except for praise and honor, and that, in pursuing these, every bodily suffering, every danger of death and exile, is to be considered of little account, I would never have exposed myself, for your safety, to so many and such great struggles, and to the daily attacks of depraved men.

annotations.significance: These terms represent the core values Cicero emphasizes as the primary goals in life. They reflect the Roman ideal of striving for reputation and moral integrity, which are central to his argument.
This phrase highlights Cicero's willingness to endure physical suffering for the sake of his principles. It underscores the idea that personal sacrifice is necessary in pursuit of honor and praise.
These dangers illustrate the risks Cicero is willing to take. They emphasize the high stakes involved in his commitment to his values and the challenges he faces in defending them.

This phrase refers to the corrupt or morally bankrupt individuals Cicero is opposing. It reflects the adversarial context of his oratory and the moral contrast he draws between himself and his opponents.
This term conveys the intensity and frequency of Cicero's conflicts. It underscores his portrayal of himself as a tireless defender of justice and honor in the face of relentless opposition.

text: Is et ipse scripsit multa praeclare et docuit alios; et cum cetera melius quam superiores, tum primus intellexit etiam in soluta oratione, dum versum effugeres, modum tamen et numerum quendam oportere servari. Ante hunc enim verborum quasi structura et quaedam ad numerum conclusio nulla erat; aut, si quando erat, non apparebat eam dedita opera esse quaesitam.
difficulty: Cicero's analysis of Isocrates's rhythmic prose revolution. 'in soluta oratione dum versum effugeres' (in prose, so long as you avoided verse) defines the boundary between poetry and prose. 'modum tamen et numerum quendam oportere servari' (yet a measure and certain rhythm ought to be maintained) introduces prose rhythm theory. 'verborum quasi structura' (a kind of structure of words) uses 'quasi' to indicate the metaphor is approximate. 'dedita opera esse quaesitam' (had been deliberately sought) reveals the paradox of artful artlessness.
translation_A: He himself also wrote many excellent things and taught others; and while he did other things better than his predecessors, he was the first to understand that even in continuous speech, while avoiding verse, a certain rhythm and meter should nonetheless be preserved. For before him, the structure of words and a certain rhythmic conclusion were non-existent; or, if they ever existed, it did not appear that they had been sought with careful effort.
translation_D: He himself also wrote many excellent works and taught others; and while he surpassed his predecessors in other respects, he was the first to understand that even in free prose (soluta oratione), while avoiding verse, a certain rhythm and measure ought nonetheless to be preserved. For before him, there was no structure of words, as it were, and no rhythmic conclusion (ad numerum conclusio); or, if there ever was one, it did not seem to have been sought out with careful effort.

annotations.significance: Highlights the individual's contributions to rhetoric and prose style, emphasizing their quality and influence.
Distinguishes prose from verse, focusing on the rhythmic qualities in non-metrical writing.
Introduces the concept of rhythmic structure in prose, emphasizing its importance alongside content.

annotations.significance: Refers to the organization of language, indicating a shift towards intentional stylistic arrangement.
Illustrates the innovation of intentional rhythmic endings in prose sentences.

source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia VII.1-2
text: Principium iure tribuetur homini, cuius causa videtur cuncta alia genuisse natura, magna, saeva mercede contra tanta sua munera, non ut sit satis aestimare, parens melior homini an tristior noverca fuerit. Ante omnia unum animantium cunctorum alienis velat opibus. Ceteris sua varie tegimenta tribuit, testas, cortices, coria, spinas, villos, saetas, pilos, plumam, pinnas, squamas, vellera; truncos etiam arboresque cortice, interdum gemino, a frigoribus et calore tutata est: hominem tantum nudum et in nuda humo natali die abicit ad vagitus statim et ploratum.
difficulty: Pliny's pessimistic anthropology. 'cuius causa videtur cuncta alia genuisse natura' (for whose sake nature seems to have produced everything else) establishes human centrality before subverting it. 'magna saeva mercede' (at a great, cruel price) — ablative of price — introduces the paradox. 'parens melior...an tristior noverca' (a better parent or a sadder stepmother) uses a striking metaphor for nature. The catalogue of animal coverings (testas, cortices, coria...) through asyndeton contrasts with 'hominem tantum nudum' — the naked human. 'abicit' (throws down) is deliberately violent.
translation_A: The beginning is rightly attributed to man, for whose sake it seems that nature has produced all other things, with a great and harsh reward in return for his great gifts, so as not to judge whether a better parent or a sadder stepmother has been to man. Before all else, he covers one of all living things with the resources of others. He grants the others their own coverings in various ways: shells, bark, hides, thorns, down, bristles, hairs, feathers, fins, scales, wool. He has also protected trunks and trees with bark, sometimes double, from the cold and heat. But man alone he casts naked and onto the bare ground on his birthday, immediately to wailing and tears.
translation_D: The primacy is rightly attributed to the human being, for whose sake nature seems to have produced all other things, with a great, harsh reward in return for such great gifts, so that it is not enough to judge whether nature has been a better parent or a more sorrowful stepmother to humanity. Above all, it covers all other living beings with their own resources, but it clothes the human being alone with external resources. To the others, it has granted various coverings: shells, bark, hides, spines, hair, bristles, feathers, wings, scales, wool; it has even protected tree trunks and branches with bark, sometimes double-layered, from cold and heat. But the human being alone it casts naked onto the bare ground on the day of birth, immediately to crying and weeping.

annotations.significance: Central to the passage's philosophical anthropology, highlighting the unique status of humans in nature.

text: Mundum et hoc quodcumque nomine alio caelum appellare libuit, cuius circumflexu degunt cuncta, numen esse credi par est, aeternum, inmensum, neque genitum neque interiturum umquam. Huius extera indagare nec interest hominum nec capit humanae coniectura mentis. Furor est mensuram eius animo quosdam agitasse atque prodere ausos, alios rursus occasione hinc sumpta aut his data innumerabiles tradidisse mundos.
difficulty: Pliny's cosmological prolegomenon. 'hoc quodcumque nomine alio caelum appellare libuit' (this thing which we have seen fit to call sky by another name) — a remarkably tentative opening for an encyclopedia. 'cuius circumflexu degunt cuncta' (in whose revolution all things live) uses 'circumflexu' in its literal astronomical sense. 'numen esse credi par est' (it is fitting to believe it a divine power) introduces theology obliquely. 'Furor est' (it is madness) dismisses both finite cosmologists and many-worlds theorists in one sentence.
translation_A: The world—and whatever else one might choose to call the sky—by whose encircling all things exist, should rightly be believed to be a divine power, eternal, boundless, unborn, and never to perish. It is neither in the interest of humans nor within the grasp of human conjecture to investigate the external aspects of this power. It is madness for some to have dared to measure it with their minds and proclaim its limits, and for others, seizing on this occasion or being driven by it, to have posited innumerable worlds.
translation_D: The universe—and whatever other name one might choose for the sky, by whose encircling all things are sustained—ought to be regarded as a divine power, eternal, boundless, neither born nor ever to perish. It is of no concern to humans, nor does it fall within the grasp of human mental conjecture, to investigate its outer parts. It is madness that some have dared to conceive and reveal its measure, while others, taking occasion from this or similar ideas, have posited innumerable worlds.

text: Num alio genere Furiarum declamatores inquietantur, qui clamant: 'Haec vulnera pro libertate publica excepi; hunc oculum pro vobis impendi: date mihi ducem qui me ducat ad liberos meos, nam succisi poplites membra non sustinent'? Qui inter haec nutriuntur, non magis sapere possunt quam bene olere qui in culina habitant. Levibus enim atque inanibus sonis ludibria quaedam excitando, effecistis ut corpus orationis enervaretur et caderet.
difficulty: Petronius's satire of declamatory education. 'Num alio genere Furiarum' (are they not tormented by some other kind of Furies?) opens with a rhetorical question using mythological hyperbole. The embedded declamation ('Haec vulnera pro libertate publica excepi') parodies stock rhetorical exercises. 'non magis sapere possunt quam bene olere qui in culina habitant' (they can no more be wise than those who live in a kitchen can smell good) is a brilliantly vulgar simile. 'corpus orationis enervaretur et caderet' (the body of speech was emasculated and collapsed) uses the medical/bodily metaphor central to Roman rhetorical criticism.
translation_A: Is there another kind of Furies' declaimers who are troubled, who cry out: "I received these wounds for the sake of public liberty; I lost this eye for your benefit. Give me a leader who will lead me to my children, for my severed hamstrings cannot support my limbs"? Those who are nurtured among such things can no more possess wisdom than those who dwell in the kitchen can smell good things. For by exciting certain mockeries with trivial and empty sounds, you have caused the body of oratory to be weakened and to fall.
translation_D: "Or are declamators harassed by another kind of Furies, who cry out: 'I received these wounds for the sake of public liberty; I spent this eye for you: give me a leader who will guide me to my children, for my severed hamstrings no longer support my limbs'? Those who are nourished by such things can no more think clearly than those who live in the kitchen can smell well. For you have achieved nothing but empty, trifling sounds, stirring up certain mockeries, and so you have caused the body of oratory to be weakened and to fall."

annotations.significance: Used metaphorically to describe the torment or harassment of declamators, setting a critical tone for their exaggerated oratory tactics.
Refers to practitioners of declamation, a rhetorical exercise. The passage critiques their methods as emotionally manipulative and intellectually shallow.

Used to describe physical disability. The image mocks the declamators' exaggerated claims of sacrifice and weakness.

text: Iam Trimalchio eadem omnia lusu intermisso poposcerat feceratque potestatem clara voce, si quis nostrum iterum vellet mulsum sumere, cum subito signum symphonia datur et gustatoria pariter a choro cantante rapiuntur. Ceterum inter tumultum cum forte paropsis excidisset et puer iacentem sustulisset, animadvertit Trimalchio colaphisque obiurgari puerum ac proicere rursus paropsidem iussit.
difficulty: Petronius's mock-epic dinner narrative. 'lusu intermisso' (the game having been interrupted) uses an ablative absolute for trivial action. 'feceratque potestatem clara voce' (had given permission in a loud voice) parodies legal/military language for wine-serving. 'gustatoria pariter a choro cantante rapiuntur' (appetizers are snatched away in unison by a singing chorus) achieves comic bathos. 'paropsis' (side-dish) is a Greek loan word marking Trimalchio's pretensions. 'colaphisque obiurgari puerum ac proicere rursus paropsidem iussit' (ordered the boy punished with slaps and the dish thrown back down) reveals his grotesque values.
translation_A: Now Trimalchio, having interrupted the game, had already demanded and arranged with a clear voice that anyone among us who wished could take honey wine again, when suddenly a signal was given by the orchestra, and the appetizers were simultaneously snatched away by the singing choir. However, during the commotion, when a serving dish had accidentally fallen and a slave had picked it up, Trimalchio noticed it, scolded the slave with blows, and ordered him to throw the serving dish back down.
translation_D: Now Trimalchio, interrupting the game, had already demanded and arranged with a clear voice that anyone among us who wished to take mulsum again should do so, when suddenly the signal of the orchestra was given, and the appetizers were snatched away together by the singing chorus. Meanwhile, amidst the commotion, when the serving dish had fallen by chance and the boy had picked it up as it lay, Trimalchio noticed and had the boy scolded with slaps, and he ordered the dish to be thrown back again.

annotations.significance: Indicates a pause in the entertainment or festivities, highlighting Trimalchio's control over the proceedings and his tendency to interject dramatically.

Signifies the use of music to orchestrate the banquet's events, emphasizing the theatrical and overly elaborate nature of Trimalchio's hospitality.

text: Accessi confinium mortis et calcato Proserpinae limine per omnia vectus elementa remeavi, nocte media vidi solem candido coruscantem lumine, deos inferos et deos superos accessi coram et adoravi de proximo. Ecce tibi rettuli quae, quamvis audita, ignores tamen necesse est.
difficulty: Apuleius's account of Lucius's Isis initiation — the most important ancient description of mystery religion experience. 'confinium mortis' (the boundary of death) describes ritual death. 'calcato Proserpinae limine' (having trodden upon Proserpina's threshold) uses the ablative absolute for descent to the underworld. 'per omnia vectus elementa remeavi' (carried through all the elements I returned) compresses a cosmic journey. 'nocte media vidi solem candido coruscantem lumine' (at midnight I saw the sun gleaming with white light) is the central paradox. 'quamvis audita ignores tamen necesse est' (though heard, you must necessarily not understand) enforces secrecy.
translation_A: I approached the boundary of death and, having trodden upon Proserpina's threshold, traversed all the elements and returned. In the middle of the night, I saw the sun shining with bright light; I approached the gods below and the gods above, and worshiped them from nearby. Behold, I have brought back to you things which, although heard, you must nevertheless ignore.
translation_D: I approached the boundary of death and, having trodden upon Proserpina's threshold, was carried through all elements and returned. In the middle of the night, I saw the sun shining with bright light, approached the gods below and the gods above face to face, and worshipped them from a close distance. Behold, I have brought back to you things which, although heard, you must nevertheless ignore.

annotations.significance: This phrase signifies the threshold between life and death, emphasizing the protagonist's journey into the underworld. It underscores the liminal state of being between the living and the dead, a common theme in mystery religions and Apuleian narrative.

Proserpina, as queen of the underworld, represents the transition into the realm of the dead. This phrase highlights the protagonist's symbolic death and initiation into the mysteries, a key element in mystery cult narratives.

text: Vives autem beatus, vives in mea tutela gloriosus, et cum spatium saeculi tui permensus ad inferos demearis, ibi quoque in ipso subterraneo semirutundo me, quam vides, Acherontis tenebris interlucentem Stygiisque penetralibus regnantem, campos Elysios incolens ipse, tibi propitiam frequens adorabis.
difficulty: Isis's promise to Lucius of afterlife protection. 'spatium saeculi tui permensus' (having traversed the span of your age) uses an elaborate periphrasis for death. 'subterraneo semirutundo' (subterranean half-rotunda) is a architectural neologism for the underworld's vault. 'Acherontis tenebris interlucentem' (shining through the darkness of Acheron) creates an oxymoron of divine light in the underworld. 'Stygiisque penetralibus regnantem' (ruling in the Stygian inner sanctums) piles up mythological geography. Apuleius's Africitas (African Latin style) is evident in the baroque accumulation.
translation_A: But you will live blessed, you will live gloriously under my protection, and when you have measured out the span of your life and are sent down to the underworld, there too, in that very subterranean half-ruined place, you will frequently worship me, whom you see shining through the darkness of Acheron and reigning in the Stygian depths, dwelling in the Elysian fields, and propitious to you.
translation_D: But you will live blessed, you will live glorious under my protection, and when you have traversed the span of your worldly existence and are borne down to the underworld, even there, in that subterranean half-ruin, I, whom you see, shining through the darkness of Acheron and reigning in the innermost sanctuaries of the Styx, dwelling myself in the Elysian Fields, you will frequently worship me as one who is favorable to you.

annotations.significance: Indicates a state of divine bliss or happiness, emphasizing the speaker's promise of eternal joy and divine favor.
Highlights the speaker's role as a divine protector, reinforcing the idea of divine care and sovereignty.
Refers to the paradise of the blessed in the afterlife, underscoring the speaker's power to grant a glorious afterlife.
Emphasizes the reciprocal relationship between the worshipper and the deity, where devotion ensures divine favor.

text: Quoniam igitur quae sit imperfecti, quae etiam perfecti boni forma uidisti, nunc demonstrandum reor quonam haec felicitatis perfectio constituta sit. In quo illud primum arbitror inquirendum, an aliquod huiusmodi bonum quale paulo ante definisti in rerum natura possit exsistere, ne nos praeter rei subiectae ueritatem cassa cogitationis imago decipiat. Sed quin exsistat sitque hoc ueluti quidam omnium fons bonorum negari nequit.
difficulty: Boethius's ontological argument for the supreme Good. 'quae sit imperfecti quae etiam perfecti boni forma' (what is the form of imperfect and also of perfect good) sets up the Platonic framework. 'ne nos praeter rei subiectae ueritatem cassa cogitationis imago decipiat' (lest a hollow image of thought deceive us beyond the truth of the underlying reality) anticipates the ontological objection. 'ueluti quidam omnium fons bonorum' (as it were a certain fountain of all goods) uses the Neoplatonic emanation metaphor. The passage bridges Platonic, Aristotelian, and Neoplatonic metaphysics in late Latin.
translation_A: Since, therefore, you have seen what pertains to the imperfect and also the form of the perfect good, I now think that it must be shown where this perfection of happiness is established. In this regard, I believe that the first thing to be investigated is whether any such good as you defined a little while ago can exist in the nature of things, lest a vain image of thought deceive us beyond the truth of the subject. But that it does exist and is, as it were, a certain source of all goods cannot be denied.
translation_D: Since, therefore, you have seen both the form of the imperfect and the form of the perfect good, I now think it must be demonstrated where this perfection of happiness is established. In this regard, I first judge it necessary to inquire whether any such good, as you defined a little earlier, can exist in the nature of things, lest an empty mental image deceive us beyond the truth of the subject. But that such a good exists and is, as it were, a fountainhead of all goods cannot be denied.

text: Geometria autem plura praesidia praestat architecturae; et primum ex euthygrammis circini tradit usum, e quo maxime facilius aedificiorum in areis expediuntur descriptiones normarumque et librationum et linearum directiones. Item per opticen in aedificiis ab certis regionibus caeli lumina recte ducuntur. Per arithmeticen vero sumptus aedificiorum consummantur, mensurarum rationes explicantur, difficilesque symmetriarum quaestiones geometricis rationibus et methodis inveniuntur.
difficulty: Vitruvius's curriculum for architects mixing Latin and Greek technical terminology. 'euthygrammis' (straight-line constructions) is a Greek loan left untranslated. 'normarumque et librationum et linearum directiones' (the directions of set-squares, levels, and lines) lists surveying tools. 'ab certis regionibus caeli lumina recte ducuntur' (lights are correctly drawn from certain regions of the sky) describes orientation for natural lighting. 'symmetriarum quaestiones geometricis rationibus et methodis' mixes Greek and Latin technical language. The entire passage demonstrates the challenge of rendering Greek techne in Latin prose.
translation_A: Geometry, however, provides more support to architecture; and first, it imparts the use of the compass from straight lines, from which the descriptions, norms, leveling, and line alignments of buildings are most easily prepared on sites. Also, through optics, in buildings, light is correctly directed from certain regions of the sky. Through arithmetic, indeed, the costs of buildings are calculated, the principles of measurements are explained, and difficult questions of symmetry are resolved by geometric principles and methods.
translation_D: Geometry, however, provides architecture with numerous supports; and first, it provides the use of the compass for straight lines, from which the descriptions of buildings in open spaces, along with the norms and leveling, are most easily expedited. Similarly, through optics, light is correctly directed in buildings from specific regions of the sky. Through arithmetic, however, the costs of buildings are calculated, the principles of measurements are explained, and difficult problems of symmetry are solved by geometric reasoning and methods.

text: Iisdemque temporibus in tres partes medicina diducta est, ut una esset quae victu, altera quae medicamentis, tertia quae manu mederetur. Primam Διαιτητικήν, secundam Φαρμακευτικήν, tertiam Χειρουργίαν Graeci nominarunt. Eius autem, quae victu morbos curat, longe clarissimi auctores etiam altius quaedam agitare conati, rerum quoque naturae sibi cognitionem vindicarunt, tamquam sine ea trunca et debilis medicina esset.
difficulty: Celsus's history of medicine embedding untranslated Greek terms (Διαιτητικήν/Φαρμακευτικήν/Χειρουργίαν) in Latin syntax. 'quae victu...quae medicamentis...quae manu mederetur' tripartition uses three different ablatives of means. 'altius quaedam agitare conati' (having attempted to investigate certain things more deeply) describes the Dogmatist physicians' philosophical ambitions. 'rerum quoque naturae sibi cognitionem vindicarunt' (they also claimed for themselves knowledge of the nature of things) links medicine to Lucretian natural philosophy. 'trunca et debilis' (truncated and feeble) uses a vivid bodily metaphor for incomplete knowledge.
translation_A: At the same time, medicine was divided into three parts, so that one was concerned with diet, another with medications, and the third with manual treatment. The Greeks named the first ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΙΚΗΝ (Dietetic), the second ΦΑΡΜΑΚΕΥΤΙΚΗΝ (Pharmacetic), and the third ΧΕΙΡΟΥΡΓΙΑΝ (Surgery). Moreover, the most renowned authors of the part that heals diseases through diet attempted to explore certain matters more deeply and also claimed knowledge of natural science for themselves, as if medicine without it were incomplete and weak.
translation_D: At the same time, medicine was divided into three parts, so that one part would be that which heals through diet, another through medications, and the third through manual treatment. The Greeks named the first part ΔΙΑΙΤΗΤΙΚΗΝ (Dietetics), the second ΦΑΡΜΑΚΕΥΤΙΚΗΝ (Pharmacetics), and the third ΧΕΙΡΟΥΡΓΙΑΝ (Surgery). Moreover, of that branch which heals diseases through diet, the most renowned authors also attempted to delve deeper into certain matters, and they also claimed knowledge of the nature of things for themselves, as if without it medicine would be incomplete and weak.

text: Cetera non dissimulanda erunt agrorum cultori praecepta rusticationis, quae cum plurima tradiderint Poeni ex Africa scriptores, multa tamen ab his falso prodita coarguunt nostri coloni, sicut Tremelius, qui querens id ipsum tamen excusat, quod Italiae et Africae solum caelumque diversae naturae nequeat eosdem proventus habere.
difficulty: Columella's engagement with Carthaginian agricultural science (Mago). 'Poeni ex Africa scriptores' (Punic writers from Africa) refers to the translated Carthaginian agricultural manual. 'falso prodita coarguunt nostri coloni' (our farmers refute things handed down falsely) uses 'coarguunt' — a forensic verb applied to farming. 'solum caelumque diversae naturae' (soil and climate of different nature) introduces the concept of terroir. The sentence structure embeds a quote-within-a-quote (Tremelius's complaint and excuse) in a remarkably compressed period.
translation_A: The remaining precepts of rustic cultivation should not be hidden from the farmer, which, although the Punic writers from Africa have handed down many, nevertheless, many things falsely revealed by them are refuted by our colonists, such as Tremelius, who, complaining about this very thing, nevertheless excuses it because the soil and climate of Italy and Africa, being of different natures, cannot have the same yields.
translation_D: The remaining precepts of rural skills, which ought not to be concealed, will be clear to the cultivator of fields, which, although the Carthaginian writers from Africa have handed down many things, nevertheless, many things falsely presented by them are refuted by our colonists, as, for example, Tremelius, who complains about this very thing but nonetheless excuses it, because the soil and climate of Italy and Africa, being of different natures, cannot produce the same yields.

text: Cum ad instruendam rei militaris scientiam unus ex numero studiosorum eius accesserim eique destinato, quantum cura nostra valuit, satisfecisse visus sim, deberi adhuc institutae arbitror operae, ut sollertia ducum facta, quae a Graecis una στρατηγημάτων appellatione comprehensa sunt, expeditis amplectar commentariis. Ita enim consilii quoque et providentiae exemplis succincti duces erunt, unde illis excogitandi generandique similia facultas nutriatur.
difficulty: Frontinus's preface embedding Greek στρατηγημάτων in a Latin period of extraordinary length. 'cum...accesserim...satisfecisse visus sim' (since I have approached...and seem to have satisfied) uses the perfect subjunctive in a complex cum-clause. 'deberi adhuc institutae...operae' (it is still owed to the work undertaken) personifies the obligation. 'expeditis amplectar commentariis' (I shall embrace them in concise notebooks) — 'expeditis' modifying 'commentariis' means 'freed from encumbrance.' 'excogitandi generandique similia' (of devising and generating similar things) uses gerundive pairs for creative military thinking.
translation_A: When I approached one of his students to instruct him in the science of military affairs and seemed to have satisfied his needs as much as my care allowed, I still believe that I owe further instruction to the task I undertook. This is to embrace the clever deeds of commanders, which the Greeks have encompassed under the single term "stratagems," with clear commentaries. For in this way, leaders will be equipped with concise examples of counsel and foresight, from which the ability to devise and create similar strategies may be nurtured.
translation_D: When I undertook the task of instructing in the science of military matters and, as far as my care could achieve, satisfied one of my students who had approached me for this purpose, I still consider myself obligated to continue the work I have begun. For this reason, I shall compile the strategic deeds of commanders, which the Greeks encompass with the single term "stratēgemata" (strategic deeds), into concise commentaries. In this way, leaders will be equipped not only with examples of strategy but also of foresight, from which they may cultivate the ability to devise and generate similar actions.

text: Postero die profectus adversa ripa Rhodani mediterranea Galliae petit, non quia rectior ad Alpes via esset, sed quantum a mari recessisset minus obvium fore Romanum credens, cum quo priusquam in Italiam ventum foret non erat in animo manus conserere. Quartis castris ad Insulam pervenit. Ibi Isara Rhodanusque amnes diversis ex Alpibus decurrentes, agri aliquantum amplexi confluunt in unum; Insulae nomen inditum.
difficulty: Livy's narrative of Hannibal's Alpine approach. 'adversa ripa Rhodani' (up the opposing bank of the Rhône) uses 'adversa' in its directional sense. 'non quia rectior ad Alpes via esset sed quantum a mari recessisset' nests a comparative clause within a causal one. 'manus conserere' (to join hands = engage in battle) is a military idiom. 'agri aliquantum amplexi' (having embraced a fair extent of land) personifies rivers. The geographical precision requires knowledge of Alpine topography. The entire passage exemplifies Livian periodic structure at its most elaborate.
translation_A: On the next day, he set out and made for the inland regions of Gaul along the opposite bank of the Rhone, not because the route was more direct to the Alps, but because he believed that the farther he withdrew from the sea, the less likely he would encounter the Romans, with whom he had no intention of engaging before arriving in Italy. He arrived at the Island on the fourth day. There, the rivers Isère and Rhone, flowing down from different parts of the Alps, after embracing some territory, converge into one; the name of the Island was given to it.
translation_D: On the next day, he set out for the inland region of Gaul (away from the Mediterranean) along the opposite bank of the Rhone (Rhodani), not because it was a more direct route to the Alps (via), but believing that the farther he withdrew from the sea, the less likely he would encounter Romans (obvium), with whom he had no intention of engaging before reaching Italy. He arrived at the Island in the fourth camp (castris). There, the rivers Isara (Isara) and Rhone (Rhodanusque), flowing down from different parts of the Alps, having embraced a considerable amount of land, converge into one; the name Island (Insula) was given to it.

text: Et Venus in silvis iungebat corpora amantum; conciliabat enim vel mutua quamque cupido vel violenta viri vis atque inpensa libido vel pretium, glandes atque arbita vel pira lecta. Et manuum mira freti virtute pedumque venabant silvestria saecla ferarum missilibus saxis et magno pondere clavae; multaque vincebant, vitabant pauca latebris.
difficulty: Lucretius's primitive anthropology. 'Venus in silvis iungebat corpora amantum' (Venus joined lovers' bodies in the forests) mythologizes animal coupling. The tricolon 'vel mutua cupido / vel violenta viri vis / vel pretium glandes' (mutual desire / male violence / bribes of acorns) offers a disturbingly frank catalogue of sexual motivation. 'arbita' (arbutus berries) is a rare botanical term. 'silvestria saecla ferarum' (the woodland race of beasts) uses 'saecla' unusually for 'breeds.' 'vitabant pauca latebris' (they avoided few things by hiding) implies early humans were more hunter than hunted.
translation_A: And Venus was joining the bodies of lovers in the woods; for she brought them together either through mutual desire or the violent force of a man and unrestrained lust, or through gifts—acorns, arbutus berries, or chosen pears. And relying on the remarkable strength of their hands and feet, they hunted the wild beasts of the forest with stone missiles and heavy clubs; they overcame many, and a few they avoided by hiding.
translation_D: And Venus in the forests was joining the bodies of lovers, for she was bringing together either mutual desire or the violent force of men and lavish passion, or payment, acorns and berries or chosen pears. And relying on the wondrous strength of hands and feet, they hunted the wild ages of beasts with missiles of stones and heavy clubs; and they overcame many things, but avoided a few by hiding.

text: Iam dies alibi, illic nox omnibus noctibus nigrior densiorque; quam tamen faces multae variaque lumina solvebant. Placuit egredi in litus, et ex proximo aspicere, ecquid iam mare admitteret; quod adhuc vastum et adversum permanebat. Ibi super abiectum linteum recubans semel atque iterum frigidam aquam poposcit hausitque. Deinde flammae flammarumque praenuntius odor sulpuris alios in fugam vertunt, excitant illum.
difficulty: Pliny's eyewitness account of Vesuvius's eruption (79 AD). 'dies alibi illic nox omnibus noctibus nigrior densiorque' (daylight elsewhere, there a night blacker and thicker than all nights) — a stunning oxymoron of daytime darkness. 'ecquid iam mare admitteret' (whether the sea would yet permit) uses the subjunctive to express tentative hope. 'super abiectum linteum recubans' (lying back on a spread-out sheet) provides domestic detail amid catastrophe. 'flammarumque praenuntius odor sulpuris' (the prophetic smell of sulphur preceding the flames) uses the rare adjective 'praenuntius.' The shift between past tenses creates urgency.
translation_A: Already elsewhere it was day, but there night was darker and thicker than all other nights; yet many torches and various lights dispelled it. It pleased him to go out onto the shore and to look from a nearby point whether the sea would now admit anything, which was still vast and rough. There, lying on a thrown-off linen cloth, he once and again asked for cold water and drank it. Then the smell of sulfur, a herald of flames and fire, turned others to flight and roused him.
translation_D: Now elsewhere it was day, but there a night darker and denser than all other nights; yet many torches and varied lights dispelled it. It pleased him to go out onto the shore and to look from close up whether the sea now admitted anything; but it was still vast and opposing. There, lying on a thrown-down cloth, he once and again asked for cold water and drank it. Then the smell of sulfur, heralding flames and fire, turned others to flight and roused him.

text: Nil igitur mors est ad nos neque pertinet hilum, quandoquidem natura animi mortalis habetur. Et velut anteacto nil tempore sensimus aegri, ad confligendum venientibus undique Poenis, omnia cum belli trepido concussa tumultu horrida contremuere sub altis aetheris oris, in dubioque fuere utrorum ad regna cadendum omnibus humanis esset terraque marique.
difficulty: Lucretius's most famous argument: death is nothing to us. 'Nil igitur mors est ad nos neque pertinet hilum' (death therefore is nothing to us and concerns us not a whit) — 'hilum' is an archaic word for the smallest possible quantity. 'anteacto nil tempore sensimus aegri' (we felt nothing painful in past time) grounds the argument in prenatal non-existence. The analogy to the Punic Wars ('ad confligendum venientibus undique Poenis') historicizes the cosmic argument. 'horrida contremuere sub altis aetheris oris' (shuddered horribly beneath the high shores of the sky) uses epic diction for world-historical catastrophe. 'utrorum ad regna cadendum' (under whose dominion all must fall) is an indirect question within the historical digression.
translation_A: Death, therefore, is nothing to us and does not concern us at all, since the nature of the soul is considered mortal. And just as we feel no pain at a time long past, when the Carthaginians were coming from all sides to engage in battle, all things, shaken by the tumult of war, trembled horribly under the high heavens, and it was uncertain which side would fall into the power of the other, over all human affairs, on land and sea.
translation_D: Death, therefore, is nothing to us and does not concern us at all, seeing that the soul is held to be mortal by its very nature. Just as we feel no pain at a past time when the Carthaginians were coming from all sides to battle, and all things, shaken by the tumult of war, trembled dreadfully beneath the high heavens, and it was uncertain whose rule would prevail over all human realms on land and sea.
